11. However, in support of his assertion, the learned counsel cited a plethora of decisions firstly, in the case of Assessing Officer, Narayanganj Ranges vs Burmah Eastern Limited reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 450 = 34 DLR (AD) 29, an unreported judgment passed in civil appeal No. 54 of 2001 that corresponds civil petition for leave to appeal No. 9 of 2001 dated 03-12-2003 both appeared in an online legal journal named, Manupatra; another unreported judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 50 of 1985 dated 09-6-1988 also appeared in Manupatra; decision in the case of Farid Uddin Mahmud vs Md Saidur Rahman, reported in 2011 BLD (AD) 79; judgment passed dated 9-4-1997 in Civil Appeal No. 5 of 1996 of the Appellate Division appeared in Manupatra; decision in the case of Abu Jafar Md Nurul Islam vs DG, Department of Environment, Government of Bangladesh reported in 56 DLR I and decision reported in 15 BLC 770. With above submissions and relying on those decisions, the learned counsel finally prays for making the Rule absolute. 

 21. Per contra, Mr M. Khaled Ahmed, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent No. 6 at first filed an application for vacating the order of stay mainly basing on the provision of section 14 of the Ain asserting that, writ will only lie when there remains no efficacious remedy but in the present case, section 14 of the Ain clearly provides the provision of appeal against the grievance of the petitioner and it is clear that without exhausting the said provision of appeal the instant writ has been filed and even though the petitioner has not made any statement as to why he has not resorted to appeal, so the writ petition is not maintainable and the Rule liable to be discharged. 

 29. The learned counsel next submits that, it is the constitutional obligation of the government to ensure the right of people as regard to the protection and improvement of environment for the best welfare of its citizen and in case of breach thereof it should be enforced under Article 102 of the Constitution and this Hon'ble Court is the only instrumental for protecting such right to the affected people and for the welfare of the state as well as its citizen at large, but in the name of producing bi-product what the petitioner is doing totally goes against the express provision enumerated in Article 18A of our Constitution and therefore, the impugned letter has rightly been issued which is liable to be sustained. 

 30. However, to buttress the above submissions, the learned counsel has placed his reliance to a slew of decisions, in the case of Controller of Examinations, University of Dhaka Mahinuddin reported in 44 DLR (AD) 305; in the case of Zahur Ahmed vs Commissioner of Customs reported in 51 DLR 206; in the case of Prof Nurul Amin Bepari vs Vice-Chancellor reported in 50 DLR 405; in the case of Gazi M Towfic vs Agrani Bank reported in 54 DLR (AD) 6; in the case of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) vs Artha Rin Adalat reported in 59 DLR (AD) 6; in the case of Moulana Md Abdul Kader Azadi vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 58 DLR 114; in the case of Dr. Moniuddin Farooque, Secretary General, Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA) being dead Ms Syeda Rizwana Hasan, Director (Programme) representing BELA vs Bangladesh and others reported in 55 DLR 69 and in the case of Bangladesh vs Anwar Ahmed reported in 18 BLD (AD) 281 = 51 DLR (AD) 42. The learned counsel finally prays for discharging the Rule. 

 33. In such a compelling proximate cause, we in the first place feel it expedient to figure out whether writ itself is maintainable and if on discussing legal aspect involved in this case we find the answer to the negative, we would then refrain from enter into the merit of the case. 

 41. At this, the learned counsel for the petitioner raised a question that, the respondent No. 4 has no authority to issue impugned notice by closing the petitioner's factory which can only be done by the respondent No. 2 and in that case, the respondent No. 4 is a quoram non-judice in exercising such power. To refute such assertion, the respondent Nos. 2-3 by annexing a circular as of Annexure- '9' to the supplementary-affidavit asserts that, by virtue of delegation of power by the respondent No. 2 to the respondent No. 4, the impugned notice has been issued which has perfectly been done. 

 52. Aside from that, from Annexure- 'E' to the writ petition, we also find that, when on 1-11-2017 the environment certificate of the petitioner was last renewed up to 5-4-2018, it was done giving condition of fulfilling certain requirement to be observed by the petitioner. As after expiry of the said period, the respondent No. 4 did not find any requirement supposed to be fulfilled by the petitioner and the respondent No. 2 then on 20-5-2018 has very logically issued the show cause notice (Annexure- 'J' to the writ petition). All the above facts lead us to legally assume that, the petitioner has willfully violated the provision laid down in the Ain else BGMEA or the present respondent Nos. 6 and 7 could not have raised the objection and respondent Nos. 2-3 deliberately cautioned him. Moreover, for one's hazardous wrongdoing, the surrounding industrial belt cannot suffer for years together. Keeping the importance of protecting environment from being impaired even our national Parliament has also felt it expedient to incorporate Article 18A in the Constitution. In line with the said beneficial provision set out in our Constitution meant for the welfare of the citizen and for the generation to come, the Hon'ble Appellate Division in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Mustafijur Rahman set-out the following proposition which has been reported in 72 DLR (AD) 211: 

 53. Ongoing through the said ratio, we also find that, the analogy set at rest is squarely applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case as well so far as regards to protect the environment at any place not to say in the industrial area. 

 54. Now let us examine how far the decision cited by the learned counsel for the petitioner be applicable in filing and maintaining the instant writ petition. It is to be mention here that, insofar as regards to the decision reported in 58 DLR 405 (as cited by the learned counsel for the petitioner), the learned counsel for the respondent No. 6 submits that, in that decision, learned senior counsel for the petitioner had earlier canvassed for resorting alternative remedy that is to say, to file appeal while representing Dhaka University and he won the said writ petition on the point of maintainability, though in the instant writ petition, the learned senior counsel though took stand for the opposite. Controverting the said view of the learned counsel of the respondent No. 6, Mr Mahbub Shafique, the learned counsel for the petitioner then referred to a judgment dated 3-12-2003 passed in civil appeal No. 54 of 2001 corresponding to civil petition for leave to appeal No. 9 of 2001 appeared in the online legal journal named "Manupatra" where writ is found to be maintainable despite of having alternative remedy and his senior counsel had also represented Dhaka University and made similar assertion what he put forward in the case reported in 58 DLR 405. But the learned counsel has now been relying on subsequent decision as passed by the Appellate Division. 

 55. We have also gone through the said judgment passed in civil appeal No. 54 of 2001 corresponding to civil petition for leave to appeal No. 9 of 2001 but what has been settled in that judgment is, if any action taken beyond the provision of law or derogation thereof, in that case, alternative remedy will not stand in the way of invoking writ jurisdiction. But the case in hand, we don't find that, the respondent No. 4 who passed the impugned notice lacks any jurisdiction or it caused any derogation to exert authority. So the decision upon which the learned counsel puts his emphasis has got no relevance with the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

 57. The learned counsel for the petitioner then referred another judgment dated 9-6-1988 so appeared in the online legal journal 'Manupatra' in writ petition No. 50 of 1985, where it has been held that, "the provisions of Customs Act is a matter concerning the interpretation of an act of legislature- It was therefore fit and proper that the petitioner had agitated the matter in the original constitutional jurisdiction rather than leave it to be decided by the executive authority who is the appellate authority". This decision has also got no substantive implication in this case as well, as what has been held in the decision in particular, in paragraph No. 20 thereof, has subsequently been reversed by our Hon'ble Appellate Division in the judgment which has been reported in 20 BLC (AD) 64 as well as 52 DLR (AD) 149 and in those decisions, it has been settled once for all that, without resorting to the appellate authority, the aggrieved party cannot resort to writ jurisdiction challenging any action taken by the customs authority. So that very decision as relied by the petitioner as has been overruled by those two decisions by our Hon'ble Appellate Division and hence, it has no manner of application in the instant writ petition. 

 59. The learned counsel has next referred another judgment dated 9-4-1997 appeared in the online legal journal 'Manupatra' in civil appeal No. 5 of 1996 where we find that very appeal was preferred against the judgment passed by a Special Tribunal in an Arms Case but he could not prefer the same within the statutory period of time for which he at first resorted to the provision of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and then invoked writ jurisdiction and both the miscellaneous case and the writ petition were dismissed in limini and challenging the judgment passed in writ petition, the convict-appellant then preferred civil appeal and in the appeal, the Hon'ble Appellate Division found that the learned Judge who passed the impugned conviction has got no jurisdiction that is, the learned Judge passed judgment without having any jurisdiction (Quoram non-judice) but in the instant case we overwhelmingly find that, the writ petitioner has ever raised any question as regards to the jurisdiction of the respondent No. 4 in issuing impugned letter and it has been found from the provision of the Ain of 1995 and that of Rule of 1997 that, there has been an appellate authority and respondent No. 4 has got the authority to issue the impugned notice. 

 60. The learned counsel for the petitioner has also referred a decision reported in 56 DLR 1, where it has been held that, without giving any show cause notice no final order can be passed under the provision of sections 4(3), 8, 10 and 11 of the Ain and that of the Rule 5 but in the instant case, it has repeatedly been found that, before issuing the impugned notice the petitioner was served with several show cause notice and since the petitioner did not take any appropriate measure to correct the pollution caused by him as has been found by the respondent No. 2 and repeated allegations have been levelled against the petitioner and since show cause notice is found to have issued before passing the impugned notice, so that very decision has got no manner of application in this case. 

 61. The last decision so have been cited by the learned counsel for the petitioner reported in 15 BLC 770 where it has been held that, if the impugned action is wholly without jurisdiction in the sense, of not being authorized by the statute or is in violation of a constitutional provision, a writ petition will be maintainable. But in the instant case, it has deliberately been found that, the petitioner did not raise any question as regards to the jurisdiction of the respondent No. 4 in issuing impugned notice, rather the alleged authority (whether delegation has been made or not) in issuing the same. But by filing different circulars both at the instance of respondent Nos. 2-3 by the DAG as well as the learned counsel for the respondent No. 6, it has palpably been found that, the power has been delegated by the respondent No. 2 upon the respondent No. 4 to do so, so under no circumstances, can it be said that, the respondent No. 4 has got no authority because those very circulars filed by the learned DAG as well as the learned counsel for the respondent No. 6 has not been controverted by the learned counsel for the petitioner by filing any affidavit-in-reply because it is found that there has been statutory provision providing appellate authority and the respondent No. 4 has been delegated power by respondent No. 2 to act on its behalf. So that very decision is totally inapplicable with the facts and circumstances of the instant case as well. 

 62. We have also perused the decisions cited by the learned counsel for respondent No. 6 and found that apart from decision reported in 55 DLR 69 all are related to the point of maintainability where it has been decided that under no circumstances, an aggrieved party can resort to writ jurisdiction if there has been an alternative remedy. However, the decision reported in 55 DLR 69 which is considered to be a pioneering judgment in the field of "public interest litigation" (in the case of Dr Mohiuddin Farooque vs Bangladesh and others) it has been held that: 

 "Environment Protection Act, 1995 Section 4 Both the Constitution of Bangladesh and the environmental laws enjoined the government functionaries to take adequate measures to prevent environmental pollution. It is also the constitutional obligation of the Government to ensure that the rights of the people, so very glorified under Article 18 and Article 32 of the Constitution, are vindicated and defended and the provisions of the said Act is implemented in its real sprit to protect the interest of the people. In case of any breach or lathes in this respect, such constitutional obligations can be enforced against the Government under Article 102 of the Constitution. In such a process, the Supreme Court is only instrumental under the Constitution in achieving the constitutional objectives of a welfare state." 

 63. Last but obviously not the least, from the terms of the Rule, we find that, the said Rule was issued in the form of "writ of certiorari" and definitely it is under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution—which provides "if the aggrieved party has no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law" but the case in hand, is totally otherwise where the petitioner has got alternative remedy. 

 64. From the forgoing discussion and observation, it has unequivocally proved that, the petitioner has got equally efficacious remedy. But he did not resort to and why he did so nothing has been stated in the entire writ petition. But what has been cited by the learned counsel for the petitioner in support of his submission—those all are mere exception to evade alternative remedy—which are not at all applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and those have elaborately been discussed in the penultimate paragraphs needs no repetition here. 

 65. On top of that, if this court goes beyond the express provision set out in Article 102 and 18A of our Constitution and that of the statutory provision enumerated in relevant section of the Ain of 1995 in that case, there is every likelihood to jeopardize the spirit of those provision that will result in, this court will be flooded with writ petition bypassing the alternative forum which was not the intention of the legislators who framed our sacred Constitution. 

 67. In that panorama, we can profitably rely in the case of Controller of Examinations, University of Dhaka vs Mohiuddin reported in 44 DLR (AD) 305 and in the case of Fariduddin Mahmud vs Md Saifur Rahman reported in 16 MLR (AD) 205 = 63 DLR (AD) 93. In the decisions of those cases, it has been settled that "where there is alternative remedy provided under the statute, the writ petition is not maintainable." 

 68. At the very outset, we have stated that, if we find this writ is not maintainable, we will not touch upon the merit of the case and for that obvious reason we did so.
